title: still, any more, yet, already
subtitle: Joe is still in bed / Lucy doesn't work here any more / he isn't here yet / she has already left
summary: Use still for a situation that is continuing, not ... any more for a situation that has changed, yet for something you expect to happen, and already for something that happened sooner than expected.

lesson.heading: still
lesson.text: We use **still** to say that a situation or action is continuing. It hasn't changed or stopped. Still can also mean 'in spite of this'. Still usually goes in the middle of the sentence with the verb.

examples.text: It's ten o'clock and Joe is **still** in bed.
When I went to bed, Chris was **still** working.
Do you **still** want to go away or have you changed your mind?
He has everything he needs, but he's **still** unhappy.

lesson.heading: not ... any more / not ... any longer / no longer
lesson.text: We use **not ... any more** or **not ... any longer** to say that a situation has changed. Any more and any longer go at the end of a sentence. You can write any more (2 words) or anymore (1 word). You can also use **no longer**, which goes in the middle of the sentence. We do not normally use 'no more' in this way.

examples.text: Lucy **doesn't** work here **any more**. She left last month. or Lucy doesn't work here **any longer**.
We used to be good friends, but we **aren't any more**.
Lucy **no longer** works here.
We are **no longer** friends.

left.label: still (the situation continues)
examples: Mike lost his job six months ago and is **still** unemployed.

right.label: not ... any more (the situation has changed)
examples: We used to be good friends, but we **aren't any more**.

lesson.heading: yet
lesson.text: We use **yet** mainly in negative sentences (He isn't here yet) and questions (Is he here yet?). Yet (= until now) shows that the speaker expects something to happen. Yet usually goes at the end of a sentence, and we often use it with the present perfect.

examples.text: It's 10 o'clock and Joe isn't here **yet**.
Have you decided what to do **yet**?
'Where are you going on holiday?' 'We don't know **yet**.'
Mike lost his job six months ago and hasn't found another job **yet**.
Has it stopped raining **yet**?

lesson.heading: still ... not: surprise or impatience
lesson.text: Still is also possible in negative sentences (before the negative). This is similar to 'not ... yet', but **still ... not** shows a stronger feeling of surprise or impatience.

examples.text: She said she would be here an hour ago and she **still hasn't** come.
I sent him an invitation last week. He **hasn't** replied **yet**.
examples.note: but I expect he will reply soon

examples.text: I sent him an invitation weeks ago and he **still hasn't** replied.
examples.note: he should have replied before now

lesson.heading: already
lesson.text: We use **already** to say that something happened sooner than expected. Already usually goes in the middle of a sentence or at the end.

examples.text: 'What time is Sue leaving?' 'She has **already** left.'
Shall I tell Joe what happened or does he **already** know?
I've just had lunch and I'm **already** hungry.
She's **already** left. or She's left **already**.

lesson.text: Position check: still, already and no longer go in the middle with the verb; yet, any more and any longer go at the end of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Mike lost his job a year ago and he is ___ unemployed.
exercises.explanation: The situation is continuing (he has no job), so we use still.

exercises.prompt: Amy used to work at the airport, but she doesn't work there ___.
exercises.explanation: The situation has changed, so we use not ... any more at the end of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Do you ___ live in the same place or have you moved?
exercises.explanation: Still asks whether a situation is continuing: Do you still live in the same place?
In a question about something you expect to happen, use yet at the end.

exercises.prompt: There's no need to introduce me to Joe. We've ___ met.
exercises.explanation: Something happened sooner than expected: We've already met.

exercises.prompt: I've put on weight. These trousers don't fit me ___.
exercises.explanation: The situation has changed (they used to fit), so: don't fit me any more.

exercises.prompt: Each sentence with still has a similar meaning to a sentence with not ... yet. Match them.

pairs.left: Kate is still looking for a job.
I'm still wondering what to do.

exercises.prompt: They're still repairing the road. Say the same thing with not ... yet.
exercises.answer: They haven't finished repairing the road yet.
exercises.explanation: Yet goes at the end of a negative sentence.

exercises.prompt: The plane is still waiting on the runway. Say the same thing with not ... yet.
exercises.explanation: Present perfect negative + yet at the end: It hasn't taken off yet.

exercises.statement: A few years ago Paul was interested in politics. Now he isn't. So: He is no more interested in politics.
exercises.explanation: He is no longer interested in politics. or He isn't interested in politics any more. We do not use 'no more' in this way.

exercises.statement: A few years ago Paul wanted to be a teacher, and he wants to be a teacher now. So: He still wants to be a teacher.
exercises.explanation: Correct. The situation has not changed, so still is right, and it goes in the middle with the verb.

exercises.prompt: Where does each word usually go in a sentence?
categories: In the middle, with the verb
At the end of the sentence

exercises.prompt: Mark said he'd be here at 8.30. It's 9 o'clock now and he ___ isn't here.
exercises.explanation: Still ... not (before the negative) shows surprise or impatience: he still isn't here.
